name: Wangye (Plague Lord)
domain: Exorcism, protection from plagues, patrolling the world on behalf of Heaven
description: On a beach in southern Taiwan, a wooden boat worth millions — every plank carved by hand — is set ablaze while tens of thousands watch in silence. This isn't an accident. It's the "burning of the King Boat," the grandest ritual in the south, and its star is Wangye, the Royal Lords, also called Qiansui Ye or the Imperial Inspectors who "patrol on Heaven's behalf." Wangye isn't a single deity but an entire divine clan: the Five Royal Lords, the Seven Royal Lords, the Twelve Plague Kings, and hundreds more, each bearing a different surname. Their temples crowd the coasts of Yunlin, Chiayi, Tainan, Kaohsiung, and Pingtung, where their duty is to patrol the mortal world for Heaven and drive out plague. In Donggang, Pingtung, the Welcoming the Royal Lords Festival — held once every three years — runs eight days of inviting, parading, feasting, and finally burning the King Boat, and is now a designated National Important Folk Custom. Nankunshen Daitian Temple in Tainan, meanwhile, is known as the head temple of all Wangye in Taiwan, its branch temples scattered island-wide. If you want to see Taiwanese folk religion at its most alive, spend a day at a Wangye temple.
story:
Who exactly is Wangye? Folk tradition offers at least three answers, and every one of them has drama.

The most widely told version says that during the Tang Dynasty, 360 successful scholars were sent out on an imperial inspection tour, only to perish at sea along the way. The Jade Emperor, moved by their loyalty, enfeoffed them as "Imperial Inspectors" who descend to earth in rotation to examine human conduct and expel plague — which is why Wangye come with so many different surnames.

A second version ties them to Koxinga: officers who fell in his campaigns were later honored as local guardians, and Wangye worship around Tainan and Kaohsiung often carries this thread of history.

But the version closest to ordinary life is "plague-sending." In an age when epidemics were the most terrifying of disasters, people gave the plague a face — a Wangye — built a real boat, loaded it with offerings, and sent it out to sea. Coastal residents who found such a boat drifting ashore did not dare treat it lightly: its arrival was "Heaven's will," and it had to be welcomed reverently into the village and enshrined in a new temple. Many Wangye temples in Taiwan began exactly this way, with a boat that drifted in from the tide.

Three tellings point to the same truth: in an age before modern medicine, Wangye were the people's greatest bulwark against plague.

temples.name: Donglong Temple
temples.deityStory: Famous for the triennial 'King Boat Ceremony'. The burning of the King Boat is the climax, symbolizing the expulsion of plague and evil spirits.

temples.name: Nankunshen Daitian Temple
temples.deityStory: Known as the head temple of Wangye in Taiwan. It has branches all over the island. During pilgrimage season, the scene of spirit mediums performing rituals is spectacular.

associatedTemples: Donggang Donglong Temple (Donggang Township, Pingtung County)
Nankunshen Daitian Temple (Beimen District, Tainan City)
worship:
Offerings to Wangye are chiefly fresh flowers, fruit, vegetarian dishes, and pastries; during King Boat festivals some temples also prepare the Three Sacrifices (chicken, pork, fish). Worship intensity follows each temple's principal Wangye — a different surname means a different birthday.

The real spectacle at a Wangye temple is the ritual. In the "incense-passing parade" the deity's image is carried through the neighborhoods, blessing every area it passes; in "pilgrimage," groups travel back to ancestral temples to pay respects; and Wangye worship remains famous for "spirit-medium consultation," in which a god speaks through an entranced medium — one of the few living traditions of its kind still practiced frequently in Taiwan.

During King Boat ceremonies you can join in inviting, parading, and feasting the deities, but a few points of etiquette matter: keep quiet, don't block the ritual paths, and follow the temple staff's instructions. If you want to photograph an entranced medium or the boat-burning, always clear it with the temple beforehand.
festivals:
Wangye birthday dates vary by surname. Common ones include Lord Li (lunar 4/26), Lord Chi (lunar 6/18), Lord Wu (lunar 9/15), Lord Zhu (lunar 8/15), Lord Fan (lunar 4/27), and Lord Wen (lunar 11/1). Each temple celebrates according to its primary deity's birthday.

The most representative ceremony is the **Donggang Welcoming the Royal Lords Festival** in Pingtung. Held every three years (in Chou, Chen, Wei, and Xu years of the lunar cycle), the eight-day event includes welcoming, fire-walking, parading, banqueting, and finally the climactic burning of the King Boat. It is one of Taiwan's largest religious cultural events and has been designated a National Important Folk Custom. Similar King Boat ceremonies are held at **Mailiao Gongfan Temple** (Yunlin), **Xigang Qing'an Temple** (Tainan), and **Budai Yong'an Temple** (Chiayi), with varying schedules.

During the Lunar New Year period, Wangye temples also host group worship and "Tai Sui appeasement" (安太歲) rituals — making this one of the busiest seasons for observing Wangye worship.

name: Nezha (Third Prince)
domain: Exorcism, Guardian of Children, Patron of Drivers
description: Fire wheels on his feet, a fire-tipped spear in his hand — and, these days, a neon suit and techno pounding in the background. Nezha, the Third Prince (San Tai Zi), might just be the most stylish deity in the world. He is the boy-hero of the classic Investiture of the Gods, the third son of General Li Jing, honored in the pantheon as "Marshal of the Central Altar." Unlike the solemn, bearded elders of most temples, Nezha is forever a child — belly bib, cosmic ring, flaming wheels, visibly bursting with too much energy. But don't let the cuteness fool you: as the vanguard of the spirit army, he charges in first to clear away demons, and in every temple procession his divine generals lead the parade. At the 2009 World Games opening ceremony in Kaohsiung, the "Techno Nezha" — puppet generals in neon armor dancing to electronic music — brought the house down, then went on to Shanghai, Japan, and the United States and became a signature symbol of Taiwanese culture. He's also one of the few gods worshipped in the form of a child: at festivals his generals interact with kids and hand out candy, making him perhaps the most approachable deity you'll ever meet.
story:
Nezha's story is extraordinary from the moment he's born.

Li Jing's wife was pregnant for three years and six months (no, that's not a typo), and what she delivered was a ball of flesh. Horrified, Li Jing drew his sword and cut it open — and out sprang a little boy in a belly bib, standing on wheels of wind and fire. This was Nezha.

He was a troublemaker from the start. One day he went down to the sea to cool off, turned the Dragon King's undersea palace upside down, and killed the Dragon King's own son. When the Dragon King came demanding that Li Jing hand him over, and it looked as if the whole family would suffer for it, Nezha did something staggering: he stripped the flesh from his body and the bone from his frame, returning them to his parents, severing the tie of blood and shouldering all the blame alone.

Later his master, Taiyi Zhenren, rebuilt him a new body out of lotus flowers. From then on Nezha was no longer mortal flesh but a lotus incarnation — faster, fiercer, stronger.

That "dare to act, dare to answer for it" spirit is probably why Taiwanese love him so much: he's flawed, he causes chaos, but he owns what he does.
worship:
What should you pray for? A child's safety and health, protection from evil, and drive in your work — when you need a burst of forward momentum, Nezha is your god. If your kid is a handful, you can ask him to keep an eye out too.

How to worship: offer candy, cookies, cola, and toys (Nezha is a child; he likes sweet and fun things). The Three Sacrifices are fine too, but he prefers snacks. You can be a little playful when you speak to him — no need to stand on ceremony. Some temples even let you leave a toy car on the altar as an offering, which makes Nezha's altar perhaps the most fun in all of Taiwan.

The one taboo: don't disrespect him just because he looks like a child. He is the Marshal of the Central Altar, and in the divine hierarchy his combat power is first-rate.
festivals: Nezha's birthday falls on the 9th day of the 9th lunar month. Major celebrations are held at temples across Taiwan, featuring spirit medium performances and processions. The "Techno Nezha" (Dian Yin San Tai Zi) performances have become a cultural phenomenon, appearing at international events and even the 2017 Taipei Universiade. The Xinying Taizi Temple in Tainan hosts one of the most elaborate Nezha birthday celebrations, combining traditional rituals with modern performances that showcase how ancient beliefs adapt to contemporary culture.

name: Tiger Lord
domain: Wealth, protection, guardian of children (curing mumps)
description: Walk into the temple and don't crane your neck upward — crouch down instead and look beneath the main altar table. There, wide-eyed with a gold coin clamped in its jaws, is a crouching tiger: this is the Tiger God, or Hu Ye, also called Hu Ye Gong or the "General of the Lower Altar." He began as the mount of senior gods such as the Earth God, Baosheng Dadi, and the City God, which is why he lives under the altar rather than on it — yet his incense burns as hot as any "superior's." Taiwanese come to the Tiger God for two things above all. The first is wealth: as the saying goes, "the Tiger God brings the money in," and worshippers hold coins to his mouth and pass them through the incense smoke to carry the fortune home, with especially big crowds during Lunar New Year. The second is children: folk belief holds that the Tiger God cures the childhood swelling known as "pig-head skin" (mumps) and blesses children to be bright, healthy, and shielded from harm. The Tiger Gods of Beigang Chaotian Temple, Xingang Fengtian Temple, and Dalongdong Baoan Temple are especially renowned. That an animal deity could earn a standing all his own is a sight found only in Taiwanese folk religion.
story:
How did a man-eating tiger become a god? The most popular version involves Baosheng Dadi.

Legend says that Baosheng Dadi (Wu Tao) was gathering herbs in the mountains one day when he came upon a tiger collapsed by the path, howling in agony. Looking closer, he saw a human bone lodged in its throat — the beast had killed a person, and this was its karmic retribution. Most people would have fled, but Baosheng Dadi reached in and drew the bone out, leaving only a warning: "From this day, you must never harm a human again."

The tiger, once saved, did not leave. It chose to stay at Baosheng Dadi's side as his guardian, vowing never to harm again and instead to protect humans with its supernatural strength — becoming the "Black Tiger General," the Tiger God.

Another version stars Zhang Daoling, founder of organized Taoism, who subdued a rampaging mountain tiger, converted it to the true path, and kept it as an attendant, so that it later became a guardian of temples.

A tiger that once harmed people, that could repent, cultivate itself, and finally become a god — the Tiger God's story is really about one of the gentlest beliefs in Taiwanese folk religion: that animals have spirit, and that even those who once went astray can turn good.

temples.name: Xingang Fengtian Temple
temples.deityStory: Xingang Fengtian Temple's Tiger Lord is one of the most famous in Taiwan, especially efficacious for wealth and children's health.

worship:
There's an order to worshipping the Tiger God: pay respects to the main deity first, then move to the Tiger God beneath the altar table. The offerings are the most distinctive part — raw meat and raw eggs (he is an animal deity, so raw food shows respect) and candy and cookies (he is also a guardian of children); some people bring red eggs too.

To pray for wealth: hold a coin to the Tiger God's mouth, pass it three times through the censer smoke while reciting "the Tiger God brings the money in," then take the coin home to your wallet or wealth corner — that becomes your "seed money."

To pray for a child's health: write the child's name and birth details on red paper, stick it beside the Tiger God's altar, and let the child touch his golden statue.

The Tiger God's birthday falls on the 6th of the sixth lunar month, when many temples hold celebrations — the perfect time to bring children for the "passing the Tiger God" blessing.
festivals:
**Tiger Lord's Birthday**: 6th day of the 6th lunar month. Temples that enshrine Tiger Lord — or whose main deities count him as a mount — hold ceremonies including sutra recitation, fire-walking purification, and communal banquets. The Mazu temples of Beigang Chaotian and Xingang Fengtian host particularly elaborate ceremonies, with families bringing children for the "passing through Tiger Lord" blessing ritual.

**Lunar New Year wealth-seeking**: During Lunar New Year, devotees flood temples to seek wealth blessings from Tiger Lord. Many temples distribute "seed money" — coins or red envelopes that have been blessed at the censer — for devotees to carry home and place in their wallets or wealth corners for prosperity throughout the coming year.

name: Zhusheng Niangniang
description: Trying for a baby? Pray to her. Pregnant? Pray to her. Baby finally here? Still pray to her. Zhusheng Niangniang — the Goddess of Birth, affectionately called "Zhusheng Ma" — is Taiwan's full-service goddess of parenthood, covering everything from conceiving a child to a safe pregnancy, a smooth delivery, and a child's healthy growth. In most temples she isn't the star; you'll usually find her in a side chamber of a Mazu or Guanyin temple. But walk over and look: the incense ash before her altar is sometimes piled thicker than at the main hall. Taiwan now has the lowest birth rate in the world, yet her incense hasn't thinned — if anything it burns more fervently, because every pregnancy has become more precious and every prayer more heartfelt. These days young parents also bring their children back to her, asking for little ones who are "easy to raise, rarely sick, and growing up strong." At the Zhusheng halls of Bangka Longshan Temple and Lukang Tianhou Temple, the days around her birthday are packed with people praying for a child.
story:
Beside Zhusheng Niangniang's statue you'll usually see twelve small figures cradling infants — the "Twelve Matrons," her delivery team, each with her own role in bringing children safely into the world.

The most intriguing detail is the flowers on her offering table. Before Zhusheng Niangniang there are commonly white flowers and red flowers: by tradition, white flowers mean a prayer for a boy and red for a girl (though some regions reverse it), and devotees hoping for a particular gender pay close attention to which flower they touch or receive.

The stories people pass around usually go like this: someone comes to pray for a child, absent-mindedly touches a flower, and later discovers they really are pregnant — with the baby's gender matching the color of the flower exactly.

Believe it or not. But the steady stream of families who return each year to give thanks, bringing their children to "meet" Zhusheng Niangniang, says at least one thing: on the hard road to having a child, this is the goddess Taiwanese trust most.
worship:
What to pray for: conception, a safe pregnancy, a smooth delivery, a child's healthy growth. Modern devotees also come to pray for successful IVF and assisted reproduction.

How to worship: prepare fresh flowers, four kinds of fruit, and spirit money; many people bring sesame-oil chicken with rice wine (the traditional postpartum tonic, wonderfully fitting as an offering here), and some bring tiny baby clothes or shoes to symbolize welcoming new life. When you light incense, state your name, age, and situation — whether you're trying to conceive, currently pregnant, or seeking a child's health, the clearer the better. After worship you may gently touch a flower on the table: white for a boy, red for a girl. Customs vary by region, so ask the temple staff to be sure.

The most important taboo: if your prayer for a child is answered, you must come back to give thanks and bring the child for Zhusheng Niangniang to "see." Give when you've received, and the next time will go just as smoothly.
festivals: Zhusheng Niangniang's birthday is celebrated on the 20th day of the 3rd lunar month. Temples dedicated to the goddess hold special ceremonies where couples come to pray for children or give thanks for successful pregnancies. Longshan Temple in Taipei is one of the most popular locations for worship. The celebration often includes puppet shows and traditional opera performances as entertainment for the goddess and her attendants.

name: Qingshui Zushi (Patriarch of Clear Water)
description: A black-faced statue whose nose is said to drop off on its own to sound a warning — that's Qingshui Zushi, the Patriarch of Clear Water, popularly called Zushi Gong, the Black-Faced Patriarch, or the Nose-Dropping Patriarch, and one of the most story-rich deities in Taiwan. He was born Chen Zhaoying (some traditions call him Chen Puzu), a Northern Song monk from Anxi County in Quanzhou, Fujian, who cultivated, healed, and prayed for rain at Qingshui Cave, and after his death became the guardian of the Anxi people. When Anxi–Quanzhou migrants crossed to Taiwan in the Ming and Qing, they brought him along, and he stands with the Three Mountain Kings (of the Chaozhou people) and Kaizhang Shengwang (of the Zhangzhou people) as one of the three great ancestral-homeland guardians of the early settlers. His black face comes from a legend in which mountain sprites tried to smoke him out with fire while he meditated, blackening his whole face as he sat unmoved. His three great temples are Bangka Qingshui Yan in Taipei, Sanxia Changfu Yan in New Taipei — renowned for its exquisite carving and its Sacred Pig ceremony every lunar 1/6 — and Tamsui Qingshui Yan.
story:
Nearly every chapter of Qingshui Zushi's legend comes with its own vivid picture.

Start with the black face. As Chen Zhaoying meditated in the mountains, sprites who wanted him gone set fires to smoke his face. He sat unmoving in his meditation, letting his whole face blacken, and in the end subdued the sprites through compassion alone. Ever since, every statue of the Patriarch is black-faced — that dark face a badge of being "unmoved by outer things."

Then the rainmaking. One year a severe drought struck Anxi; crops withered and the people fell into famine. Chen Zhaoying climbed the mountain himself, set up an altar, and fasted and prayed for seven days and seven nights. On the eighth day, sweet rain fell. From then on the people held Qingshui Cave to be sacred ground, and the Song court honored him four times, finally as the "Bright-Responding, Wide-Benefiting, Compassion-Salving, Beneficent Master."

In Taiwan he acquired his most famous marvel of all — the "falling nose." Legend says that whenever plague, earthquake, or war is about to strike, the nose of the Patriarch's statue drops off on its own as a warning, and Sanxia Changfu Yan is especially famous for its "Nose-Dropping Patriarch." A statue that pulls off its own nose to wake everyone up — that is how, generation after generation, Taiwanese came to place their trust in Qingshui Zushi.
associatedTemples: Sanxia Changfu Yan (Sanxia District, New Taipei City)
Manka Qingshui Yan (Wanhua District, Taipei City)
Tamsui Qingshui Yan (Tamsui District, New Taipei City)
worship:
Qingshui Zushi was originally a monk, so his offerings are chiefly vegetarian — fresh flowers, fruit, pastries, and clear tea — and it's best to avoid meat (unlike most folk deities, so take care not to get it wrong). His incense burns hottest around his birthday on lunar 1/6, with some temples also holding celebrations on lunar 5/6, his traditional "ascension day."

Common rites include the incense-passing parade, pilgrimage, and lighting blessing lamps, and the Zushi temple system also has an especially complete set of fortune sticks to draw. The most distinctive event is the Sacred Pig Competition held every lunar 1/6 at Sanxia Changfu Yan: residents raise temple pigs for several years and, on the deity's birthday, carry them to the temple to be weighed and ranked — the largest ceremony of its kind in Taiwan. It has drawn debate in recent years over animal welfare, but it remains Sanxia's most important act of faith. If you want to catch the excitement, arrive early on the morning of the 6th.
festivals:
**Qingshui Zushi's Birthday**: lunar 1/6. The most important festival in this cult, with all Patriarch temples in Taiwan holding celebrations.

**Sanxia Changfu Yan "Sacred Pig Competition"**: held annually on lunar 1/6, with several centuries of history. Residents raise temple-dedicated pigs (specifically fed to extreme weight) over several years; on the deity's birthday they are slaughtered and paraded to the temple, where they are ranked by weight. While controversial under modern animal welfare frameworks, it remains one of Taiwan's most thoroughly preserved traditional folk events.

**Patriarch's Ascension Day**: lunar 5/6. Some temples (notably Tamsui Qingshui Yan and Bangka Qingshui Yan) hold smaller secondary celebrations on this day to commemorate his death and ascension.

**Lunar New Year**: Throughout the Lunar New Year period, descendants of Anxi-Quanzhou migrants visit Patriarch temples to worship — an important opportunity for observing the persistence of migrant-religious community organization in modern Taiwan.

name: Baosheng Dadi
domain: Medicine, health, curing diseases, extending life
description: A doctor who never once took payment — a thousand years later, he's a god. Meet Baosheng Dadi, the God of Medicine, known to Taiwanese as "Da Dao Gong," born Wu Tao (the name is pronounced "Tao") in Tong'an, Fujian, during the Song Dynasty. In an age when seeing a doctor was a luxury, Wu Tao walked from village to village treating the poor and refusing a single coin, and after his death the country physician was elevated, step by step, into the deity who guards life itself. Today, when a Taiwanese family faces a frightening diagnosis, an upcoming operation, or even a sick pet, Baosheng Dadi is who they turn to. His most important temple is Dalongdong Baoan Temple in Taipei, whose annual Baosheng Cultural Festival blends deity processions with contemporary art and academic lectures. Its heritage restoration was so meticulous that in 2003 it won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award — a neighborhood temple earning a United Nations honor tells you everything about the place this healer holds in Taiwanese hearts.
story:
Baosheng Dadi's most famous feat is the "silk-thread diagnosis."

Legend says the empress once fell ill with a mysterious sickness that every imperial physician failed to cure. Word reached Wu Tao, and he was summoned to the palace — but there was a problem. In ancient China, a male doctor could not touch a woman of the court, let alone the empress. So he devised a solution: he had a silk thread tied to the empress's wrist and its other end drawn out beyond a screen to where he sat. Through nothing but that single thread and a screen, he read the pulse transmitted along the silk, diagnosed the illness precisely, and prescribed the cure that healed her. Doctor, or magician? The line blurs.

The tale Taiwanese love even more is a piece of divine gossip: the "feud" between Da Dao Gong and Mazu. Folk telling has it that Da Dao Gong once had feelings for Mazu (yes, even gods get crushes) and was turned down — after which the two took turns spoiling each other's birthdays. On the 15th of the third lunar month, Baosheng's birthday, Mazu sends rain to ruin his beard; on the 23rd, Mazu's birthday, he sends wind to wreck her makeup. So whenever the March weather turns suddenly wet and windy, Taiwanese still say with a grin, "Da Dao Gong's wind, Mazu's rain" — those two are at it again.
associatedTemples: Dalongdong Baoan Temple (Datong District, Taipei City)
worship:
What should you pray for? Recovery from illness, a successful operation, family health, a long sickness finally lifting. When someone at home is about to undergo major surgery, many people come first to tell Baosheng Dadi, just to set their hearts at ease.

How to worship: prepare the Three Sacrifices and four kinds of fruit, light incense, and state the patient's name and condition. Some devotees bring Chinese medicinal herbs such as angelica root or goji berries as offerings, a nod to the Medicine God. Many Baosheng Dadi temples keep "medicine oracles" — after casting moon blocks for a herbal prescription, you can take it to a Chinese pharmacy to fill.

There's only one taboo that really matters: a medicine oracle is meant to steady the mind, not to replace a doctor or license self-prescribing. If you're genuinely ill, see a physician — Baosheng Dadi was a doctor himself, and he would absolutely want you to get proper care.
festivals: The "Baosheng Cultural Festival" at Taipei's Baoan Temple is the premier event, featuring a month-long series of activities from March to April on the lunar calendar. Highlights include the "Fire Lion" (Fang Huo Shi) ceremony — a uniquely Taiwanese ritual found nowhere else — where a paper-and-bamboo lion packed with fireworks is set ablaze in an explosive display. Traditional arts performances, Taoist ceremonies, and a grand procession through the Dalongdong neighborhood are also featured. In 2003, Baoan Temple won the UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award, bringing international recognition to this cultural celebration.

name: Di Ji Zhu (Foundation Lord)
description: For many Taiwanese, the first thing you do in a new home isn't cook a meal — it's set a low table by the back door and say hello to an unseen "previous owner": the Di Ji Zhu, the Foundation Lord, also called Di Ling Gong or the House Spirit. Traditional belief holds that every plot of land and every dwelling carries the spirit of an earlier resident, and those who move in later must offer regular worship — to ask leave to live there and to receive the household's protection in return. The Foundation Lord is the most universally worshipped yet quietest of all Taiwanese deities: he has no grand temple, yet nearly every household honors him. His ritual is fittingly domestic in scale — the offering table faces inward, a low table stands in for an altar, and the food is ordinary home cooking, presented on the 2nd and 16th of each lunar month and at the year's festivals. Modern apartment life has let much of this fade, but one custom endures: worshipping the Foundation Lord when you move into a new home, a new resident's most basic greeting to the land's original keeper.
story:
Who is the Foundation Lord? Folk tradition offers three answers.

The most widespread is the "previous resident" theory: every plot of land was once lived on or farmed by someone, and if those original dwellers died with no one to make offerings, they attach to their former home as the Foundation Lord. Ignore him, folk belief says, and the household's luck sours — strange noises at night, objects that move on their own. Treat him with courtesy, and the Foundation Lord instead "rises" to become a guardian of the home, warding off evil on your behalf. It all turns on how you treat him.

A second explanation is bound up with Taiwan's ethnic history: during the heavy Han migration of the Ming-Zheng era, much of the newly cleared land had once been the villages or burial grounds of the Pingpu, the plains indigenous peoples. To appease the indigenous dead and show respect, Han settlers developed the worship of the Foundation Lord — an explanation especially common in Taiwan, carrying a note of ethnic reconciliation.

A third theory is more "institutional": the Foundation Lord is the household-level counterpart of the Earth God. The Earth God governs the neighborhood; the Foundation Lord governs your home — complementary offices.

Whichever version you accept, the core is the same: keep faith with those who came before on this land. That is why moving into a new home calls for worshipping the Foundation Lord — greet him first, and you can settle in with an easy mind.
worship:
Worshipping the Foundation Lord follows its own set of rules, quite unlike worship of any other deity.

Location: set the offering table at the home's back door or behind the kitchen, with the table facing inward — symbolizing the Foundation Lord facing the residents. Height: a low stool or low tea table is enough; don't use the tall altar reserved for major gods.

Offerings keep to the home-cooked line: a bowl of white rice, three cups of rice wine, three to five everyday dishes (vegetables or meat both fine), and fruit, with three sticks of incense. There's no need for the Three Sacrifices; a little "four-direction gold" or silver paper is all you burn, and not much of it.

Occasions: the 2nd and 16th of each lunar month; festivals such as New Year, Qingming, Dragon Boat, Ghost Month, Mid-Autumn, and Winter Solstice; moving into a new home (the most important — never skip it); and the groundbreaking, start, and completion of construction.

After lighting the incense, remember to say a short prayer — introduce your family, explain why you've come, and ask for protection. The whole ritual runs about 15 to 30 minutes, making it one of the most everyday acts of worship in Taiwanese family life.
festivals:
Di Ji Zhu has no specific "birthday" because the cult operates at the household level and doesn't require large-scale festivals. Important worship occasions include:

**2nd and 16th of each lunar month (做牙)**: Traditional businesses and some households worship Di Ji Zhu and Tudigong on the 2nd and 16th of every lunar month. The lunar 2nd day of the second month is called the "Head 牙" (頭牙, the year's first), and lunar 12/16 is the "Tail 牙" (尾牙, the year's last) — the latter often celebrated with employee feasts in modern Taiwan.

**Lunar New Year's Eve**: Di Ji Zhu worship at the back door on Lunar New Year's Eve, thanking the Foundation Lord for the past year's protection and praying for safety in the year ahead.

**Ghost Month (lunar 7th)**: The Ghost Festival period intensifies Di Ji Zhu worship, as families seek to ensure the household is undisturbed by wandering spirits.

**Moving-in Ceremony**: New residents perform Foundation Lord worship on the day of moving into a new home — this is the most universally maintained Di Ji Zhu ritual in modern Taiwan. The ceremony is typically led by a senior family member or, increasingly, a feng-shui master.

**Construction milestones**: When building a new home or undertaking major renovations, Di Ji Zhu worship occurs at every key stage (groundbreaking, start, completion) to ensure smooth construction.

name: Kaizhang Shengwang (Sacred King of Zhangzhou)
domain: Pioneer protection, local guardian deity, exorcism
description: A Tang Dynasty general who died thirteen centuries ago is still worshipped in Taiwanese temples today — he is Kaizhang Shengwang, the "Sacred King who Opened Zhangzhou," born Chen Yuanguang (657–711) and also known as Chen Shengwang or Shengwang Gong. Under Emperor Gaozong of Tang he was sent south to pacify Fujian, where he established prefectures and counties, promoted farming, and founded schools in what would become Zhangzhou — earning him the title "father who opened Zhangzhou." When Zhangzhou people crossed the strait during the Ming and Qing, they carried their guardian aboard: Kaizhang Shengwang stands with Mazu and Baosheng Dadi as one of the three great guardian deities of Hokkien migrants, and nearly every place Zhangzhou settlers cleared has a temple to him. Keelung Dianji Temple is the perfect example — Keelung's famous Miaokou Night Market grew up right in front of this Kaizhang Shengwang temple. Jingmei Jiying Temple in Taipei and Jingfu Temple in Taoyuan likewise bear witness to the Zhangzhou settlement of northern Taiwan, and each year on his birthday, lunar 2/15, these temples still hold grand celebrations.
story:
In 669 CE, an uprising broke out in southern Fujian, and the Tang court dispatched Chen Zheng at the head of warriors from 58 clans to pacify the region. When Chen Zheng died, command passed to his son — Chen Yuanguang, then just 21 years old.

What made this young commander remarkable was that he didn't rely on the sword alone. In Zhangzhou he built beacon towers and garrisoned troops to deter incursions, but he also introduced Central Plains farming techniques, founded schools, and used intermarriage, trade, and education to dissolve the conflict between Han and indigenous peoples — in an age when "pacifying" usually meant conquest, he chose the harder, longer road.

In 711 CE, Chen Yuanguang was killed in battle against the rebel leader Lan Fenggao, at the age of 55. Grateful for his work in opening the region, the people of Zhangzhou built temples to him of their own accord; successive dynasties heaped posthumous honors on him, and Emperor Huizong of Song bestowed the title "Loyal, Resolute, Cultured and Benevolent King," while the common people simply called him Kaizhang Shengwang, the Sacred King who Opened Zhangzhou.

A thousand years later, the descendants of Zhangzhou crossed the sea to clear land in Taiwan, facing the same strange soil and the same conflicts — and they brought Kaizhang Shengwang aboard with them. To this day many temple couplets read "Opening Zhangzhou, founding Taiwan": the pioneering spirit of a thousand years ago, carried straight onto Taiwanese ground.

temples.name: Keelung Dianji Temple
temples.deityStory: The birthplace of Keelung's famous Miaokou Night Market, dedicated to Kaizhang Shengwang and one of Keelung's most important spiritual centers.

temples.name: Taoyuan Jingfu Temple
temples.deityStory: The most important temple in central Taoyuan, witnessing the history of Zhangzhou immigrants settling in Taoyuan.

associatedTemples: Keelung Dianji Temple (Ren'ai District, Keelung City)
Taoyuan Jingfu Temple (Taoyuan District, Taoyuan City)
worship:
Kaizhang Shengwang is offered mainly fresh flowers, fruit, pastries, and clear tea, with some devotees adding the Three Sacrifices. On his birthday, lunar 2/15, the temples hold celebrations complete with sutra recitation, processions, and ceremonial feasts — the season when his incense burns brightest.

Because he is the guardian of the Zhangzhou people, many Zhangzhou-descended communities keep the tradition of "ancestral-temple pilgrimage": organizing group trips back to Zhangzhou Weihui Temple in Fujian to renew the incense, then returning to the branch temple in Taiwan. Suspended under martial law, these pilgrimages gradually resumed after it was lifted.

At temples in old Zhangzhou settlements such as Jingmei Jiying Temple in Taipei and Guangji Temple in Zhonghe, New Taipei, you can watch local elders cast moon blocks to consult the deity and light blessing lamps on his birthday — the most direct window into how Taiwan's early migrant society organized its ritual life around a shared homeland.
festivals:
**Kaizhang Shengwang's Birthday**: lunar 2/15. Temples in Zhangzhou-descended communities host elaborate ceremonies including sutra recitation, processions, banquets, and traditional opera performances (often glove-puppet theater). The largest celebrations occur at Taipei Jingmei Jiying Temple, Zhonghe Guangji Temple, and Yilan Jiaoxi Xietian Temple.

**Ancestral Temple Pilgrimage**: Some temples organize group visits to Zhangzhou Weihui Temple in Fujian around the birthday, marking an important cross-strait cultural exchange.

**Lunar New Year Group Worship**: During the Lunar New Year, Zhangzhou-descended families host group worship at local Kaizhang Shengwang temples, praying for peace and prosperity in the new year. This is one of the best opportunities for visitors to witness the cohesion of Zhangzhou-descended migrant communities in Taiwan.

name: Qi Niang Ma (Seven Mothers)
description: In Tainan, children who turn sixteen crawl through a paper pavilion on the night of Qixi — this is the "Coming of Age at Sixteen," and its guardian is Qi Niang Ma, the Seven Mothers, also known as Qixing Niangniang or the Weaving Maiden, seven celestial sisters worshipped together as protectors of children. Taiwanese tradition holds that a child who grows safely to sixteen owes it to Qi Niang Ma's care along the way. Many families "entrust" their infants to her as godchildren before their first birthday, hanging a guardian charm around the child's neck; in the year the child turns sixteen, they return on Qixi to "remove the charm" and give thanks, formally declaring the child an adult. This is why in Taiwan the seventh night of the seventh lunar month is more than a lovers' festival — it is also the day of children's protection and of coming of age. Kailong Temple in Tainan is the birthplace of the "Coming of Age at Sixteen" ceremony, and every Qixi its rituals of crawling under the Qi Niang Ma pavilion and crossing the Qi Niang Ma bridge draw crowds of families — the most complete traditional coming-of-age rite left in Taiwan.
story:
The mainstream legend of Qi Niang Ma is that of "seven fairy sisters who protect the infants of the mortal world."

As the story goes, the Heavenly Emperor had seven daughters, all compassionate and gifted at weaving. The youngest, the seventh, is the famous Weaving Maiden, known for descending to earth and falling in love with the Cowherd; the other six sisters stayed at their work in heaven.

One day the seven learned that infant mortality on earth was high and that many families had lost their little children to grief. Together they petitioned the Heavenly Emperor: they wished to descend and watch over the children of the mortal world until each grew safely up. Moved by their compassion, the Emperor granted the request and let them receive incense under the name "Qi Niang Ma." From then on each of the seven took charge of a stage of childhood — newborn, first steps, early learning, school age, and adolescence, all the way to coming of age at sixteen. This is the very origin of Taiwan's "Coming of Age at Sixteen" custom.

Another telling focuses on the Weaving Maiden herself: she guards not only children but also handicraft and women's needlework. On Qixi, traditional women would "beg for skill" — laying out offerings, threading needles, and praying to Qi Niang Ma for deft hands. The practice has grown rare on Taiwan's main island but survives on the outer islands of Kinmen and Penghu.

temples.name: Tainan Kailong Temple
temples.deityStory: The most famous Qi Niang Ma temple in Taiwan and the birthplace of the 'Coming of Age at Sixteen' ceremony.

worship:
Worship of Qi Niang Ma has traditionally been the province of women and children, and the offerings are rich with the symbolism of childhood: oil rice and sesame-oil chicken (for new life); seven kinds of flowers, seven kinds of fruit, and seven-colored cotton threads (for the seven sisters); and rouge, mirror, scissors, and needle-and-thread (an extension of the Qixi "begging for skill"). Most distinctive of all is the paper "Qi Niang Ma pavilion," burned during the rite.

Families with a child under sixteen can hold a Qixi rite each year: set out the table, burn the pavilion, and tie a "guardian charm" — a red string strung with seven Qi Niang Ma coins — around the child's neck for protection. In the year the child turns sixteen, on Qixi, comes the "releasing of the charm": the guardian charm is untied, announcing the end of childhood.

To see the full ceremony, go to Kailong Temple in Tainan: crawling three times under the Qi Niang Ma pavilion, crossing the Qi Niang Ma bridge, and giving thanks to Qi Niang Ma — walk it through once, and the child has officially "become an adult."
festivals:
**Qixi (Qi Niang Ma's Birthday)**: lunar 7/7. This is the central day of Qi Niang Ma worship — the protector of children and the day of coming-of-age ceremonies for 16-year-olds.

**Tainan Kailong Temple "Coming of Age at 16"**: Held annually on lunar 7/7 in Tainan's West-Central District, this is Taiwan's most complete and largest-scale traditional coming-of-age ritual. Activities include passing under the pavilion, crossing the bridge, and thanksgiving worship. It has been designated as intangible cultural heritage by the city of Tainan and attracts both local families and outside observers each year.

**The Begging for Skill Festival**: Traditional women on Qixi would pray to Qi Niang Ma (the Weaver Girl) for nimble hands and skilled craft. While rare in modern mainland Taiwan, the practice survives in offshore islands such as Kinmen, Penghu, and Matsu.

**Newborn Enrollment**: Many Taiwanese families bring their newborns to a Qi Niang Ma temple at one month or one year, ritually "entrusting" the child to her protection until age 16. This is a key family ritual marking the start of childhood guardianship.

name: Kuixing Ye (Star Lord of Literature)
description: When exam season arrives, one deity's offering table fills up with scallions, garlic, radishes, and rice dumplings — that's Kuixing Ye, the Star Lord of Literature, also known as Kuidou Xingjun or Da Kui Fuzi, the god who governs literary fortune, examinations, and scholarly honors. The character "Kui" (魁) means "first," and from the imperial civil examinations of old to today's high-school and national entrance exams, students hoping to "take first place" have always prayed to him. His image is the strangest in Taiwan: demon-formed with red hair, a blue face, and a golden body, a brush in one hand and a measuring vessel in the other, balanced on one leg — a living rendering of the character 魁 (ghost 鬼 plus vessel 斗) and of the lucky phrase "monopolizing the top spot." In Taiwan he is usually enshrined alongside Wenchang Dijun and Confucius; you'll find him in the rear hall of Bangka Longshan Temple, in the Kuixing Pavilion of the Tainan Confucius Temple, and at Lukang's Wenkai Academy. The imperial exams have been gone for over a century, but Kuixing hasn't lost his job — every exam season his censer is still ringed with students clutching their admission tickets.
story:
The legend of Kuixing is, at heart, a story about judging people by their looks.

A Song-era tale tells of a scholar of dazzling talent and brilliant prose who nonetheless failed the examinations again and again, all because he was so homely to look at. He refused to give up, sitting the exams over and over, until at last he placed first as Top Graduate. But at the palace audience, the emperor took one look at his face, was so startled that he considered stripping the title away.

Standing before the throne, the scholar argued with quiet dignity: "My looks may be ugly, but my learning shines like the sun and the moon. If we choose men by their faces, how shall we ever win the loyalty of the empire's scholars?" He then took up the brush on the spot and composed an essay expounding the principles of governance. The emperor, deeply impressed, judged that this man's brilliance "could indeed lead the scholars of the realm," and confirmed him as Top Graduate.

The scholar came to be venerated as Kuixing, a symbol of "choosing by talent, not by appearance." His "demon form," one tradition says, springs from that very homely face — proof that with real learning behind you, even an emperor must bow.

A second telling explains him through etymology: 魁 is built from "ghost" and "vessel," and the first four stars of the Big Dipper are together called "Kui," so Kuixing is the Dipper's head star, master of all literary fortune under heaven. Both tellings survive to this day — one about a man's grit, the other about a star in the sky.
worship:
The offerings to Kuixing are one long string of puns: scallion (蔥, "smart"), garlic (蒜, "good at reckoning"), radish (菜頭, "good fortune"), rice dumpling (粽, "to pass"), rice cake (糕, "high score"), and apple (for a "peaceful" exam) — a whole table that spells out a blessing.

Students can also bring their admission tickets and stationery to "pass through the censer," circling them three times over the incense to borrow a little of Kuixing's power. Some temples offer "Kuixing brushes" to take home, symbolizing a mind brimming with inspiration.

When you worship, it helps to name the subjects you're sitting and the scores you're after, and to say how you plan to study — Kuixing worship stresses "human–divine collaboration": the god lends his power, but the reading is still up to you. And when the results are posted and your name is on the list, remember to come back with offerings to give thanks.
festivals:
**Kuixing's Birthday**: lunar 7/7 (some temples observe lunar 5/7). The date varies by regional tradition — checking the local temple in advance is recommended. The largest celebrations occur at the Tainan Confucius Temple's Kuixing Pavilion and Lukang's Wenkai Academy.

**Major Examination Seasons**: Each year, Kuixing temples and Wenchang temples receive surges of visitors before:
- May: National High School Entrance Exam, General Scholastic Ability Test (學測)
- July: Subject Competence Test (指考), university admission decisions
- Year-end: Civil Service Special Exams, professional certification exams

Visiting one week before the exam is recommended to avoid peak crowds.

**Post-Exam Thanksgiving**: After exam results are released, students who succeeded in entering their target schools or positions often return with offerings to fulfill vows made before the exam. Around Kuixing temples, families specifically visiting for "thanksgiving" (謝恩) are a common sight.

name: Tudipo (Earth God's Wife)
domain: Family harmony, marital love, encouraging hard work
description: When people pay respects to the Earth God, many quietly skip the old woman seated beside him — that's Tudipo, the Earth God's Wife, also called the Earth Goddess or Lady Fude. Folk tradition saddles her with an unflattering reputation as the one who "won't hand out favors": legend paints her as shrewd and hard-nosed, forever warning her husband not to scatter wealth too freely among mortals. But that bad name does her wrong. What Tudipo guards is a quieter kind of blessing — family harmony, love between husband and wife, and the unglamorous but essential virtue of keeping your feet on the ground. A Taiwanese saying sums up the pair: "The Earth God opens the wealth; the Earth Goddess keeps it." One gives, one manages, and their roles complete each other; some devotees read her as the very embodiment of a household manager's wisdom. Major Earth God temples such as Checheng Fuan Temple in Pingtung, Sijie Fude Temple, and Honglu Di Nanshan Fude Temple in New Taipei all enshrine Tudipo beside her husband — a kindly old woman with her hair in a bun, holding a cane or an ingot, sitting quietly at his side. Next time you visit the Earth God, don't forget to greet her too.
story:
Why does Tudipo carry the blame for "refusing to make people rich"? A classic folk tale explains it.

When the Jade Emperor sent the Earth God down to manage a region, he asked what the Earth God wished for. Full of goodwill, the Earth God answered: "I wish for every person in the world to be wealthy and at peace."

Standing at his side, Tudipo shook her head at once. "That won't do! If everyone is wealthy, who will carry the sedan chairs later, who will till the fields, who will sweep the streets? If everyone lives in ease, how is this world supposed to run?"

The Jade Emperor heard her out and found the reasoning sound. And so the world came to have its divisions of rich and poor, high and low, each person receiving a different lot according to cause, effect, and effort — while Tudipo carried the bad name ever after, and many people simply skipped her when honoring the Earth God.

But look at it another way: where exactly is she wrong? Tudipo stands not for stinginess but for the wisdom of social order and the division of labor. Without the cold water she throws, the world would lose its reason to strive. Another version says she was originally a virtuous mortal woman, famed in life for running her household wisely and raising her children well, enthroned after death as the Earth God's consort — whichever the telling, she is that clear-eyed keeper of the home.
worship:
Tudipo is usually worshipped together with the Earth God: light incense and report your concerns to the Earth God first, then say them again to Tudipo. Offerings are mainly fresh flowers, fruit, cakes, and clear tea, and the more particular will prepare two sets, one for each.

What is she best asked for? Family harmony, love between spouses, filial children — these "household matters" are Tudipo's specialty. People moving into a new home or newly married often come to ask both deities to bless the household.

One small tip: when reporting family matters to Tudipo, speak respectfully and avoid complaining about or criticizing your relatives — folk tradition holds that Tudipo takes note of your words as a basis for later judgment. Some temples place a separate censer before her statue, so you can also worship her on her own.
festivals:
**Tudipo's Birthday**: 15th day of the 10th lunar month (some temples observe the 1st day of the 3rd lunar month). The date varies by temple tradition, so checking local temple announcements in advance is recommended.

**Earth God's Birthday**: 2nd day of the 2nd lunar month ("Tou Ya," the first festival of the lunar year) and 15th day of the 8th lunar month (Mid-Autumn). Earth God temples hold ceremonies on these days, and Tudipo is jointly worshipped. Many families also bring offerings to local Earth God temples on these dates.

**Lunar New Year**: During the Lunar New Year period, many devotees visit Earth God temples to pay respects to both the Earth God and Tudipo, praying for household peace and prosperity in the coming year.

name: Wen Wu Dazhong Ye
domain: Finding lost items, handling lawsuits, exorcising evil spirits, upholding justice
description: Through the seventh lunar month, offering tables spill from front doorways all the way to temple courtyards across Taiwan — and the guests of honor aren't gods but the "Good Brothers," the wandering dead. Presiding over this pact between the living and the departed is Wen Wu Dazhong Ye, also called Dazhong Ye or Lao Da Gong (the "Honorable Elder"). "Dazhong" means "the multitude, with no distinction of rank": the spirits of those who died in war, plague, or disaster with no descendants to make offerings are gathered together, enshrined, and given a home and a share of incense — transformed from ownerless wandering ghosts into the named and honored Dazhong Ye. It may be the gentlest idea in all of Taiwanese folk religion: that even the abandoned dead deserve dignity. Dazhong Ye temples cluster on old battlefields, in plague-stricken districts, and in remote frontier settlements, with Xinzhuang Dizang An in New Taipei among the most representative. Each year at the Ghost Month's Universal Salvation (Pudu), from a single table at a family's front door to a vast temple ceremony, all of Taiwan enacts the same tenderness: another's hunger is one's own.
story:
The story of Dazhong Ye is the disaster-history of Taiwan's early migrants.

During the Ming and Qing, Han Chinese crossed the strait to Taiwan only to be taken by miasma, plague, armed feuds, pirates, and natural calamity; many died far from home with no one to claim their bodies. Local residents — half out of compassion, half out of fear that ownerless spirits might cause trouble — began collectively burying the bones and building temples to honor them. This was the origin of the Dazhong temple.

Bangka preserves a representative tale. During the Tongzhi reign of the late Qing, plague raged through Bangka and the dead were many; Hui'an migrants from Quanzhou invited "Lingan Zunwang" — the Qingshan King — over from their homeland to suppress it. Legend says that the very night the Qingshan King's procession passed through, the plague receded, and from then on residents fused the Qingshan King with Dazhong Ye worship: the King presides while Dazhong Ye lead the host of wandering spirits, guarding Bangka together.

Another root lies in frontier memory. In places like Douliu in Yunlin and Xingang in Chiayi, tradition tells of early Han settlers and indigenous peoples locked in repeated conflict, with heavy losses on both sides; later generations built Dazhong temples and enshrined them together, asking only for local peace.

Dazhong Ye is not the legend of any single god but the embodiment of an entire migrant society's collective memory — of death, of disaster, and of reconciliation.
associatedTemples: Xinzhuang Dizang An (Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City)
worship:
Offerings to Dazhong Ye differ from those for ordinary gods. The Three Sacrifices, rice cakes, fruit, and wine are all acceptable (meat is fine), and many families prepare a whole chicken or pork knuckles — but one offering is unique to this worship: "water rice," white rice with water added, symbolizing food for the hungry wandering spirits. Some people also light "Pudu Lord lamps" to light the way for the lonely dead.

On ordinary days you can visit a Dazhong temple individually to pray for peace, deliverance from misfortune, or wealth. The seventh lunar month brings the main event, the "Universal Salvation" (Zhongyuan Pudu), held jointly by households and temples and the largest ritual gathering in all of Taiwan. In Toucheng, Yilan, there is also "Snatching the Lonely," in which competitors climb a grease-slicked tower about 12 meters high to seize the offerings at the top — a genuinely spectacular sight.

Keep the taboos firmly in mind: don't speak flippantly or laugh during worship; during Pudu don't tread on the offerings and don't say the word "ghost" — say "Good Brothers." And if you want to photograph the rites, get the temple's permission first.
festivals:
**Ghost Festival (Da Zhong Ye Pudu)**: lunar 7/15. The central festival of Da Zhong Ye worship — every Da Zhong temple and household holds **Universal Salvation** (中元普渡), broadly inviting "Good Brothers" to feast on offerings. The scale ranges from individual (a household altar at the front door) to township-level (large-scale temple ceremonies).

**Bangka Qingshan Temple Night Patrol**: held annually on lunar 10/20, 21, and 22, the "**Qingshan King Night Patrol Inspection**" (青山王暗訪夜巡) is one of Taipei's most distinctive folk events. The processional party patrols Bangka by night, with continuous fireworks and percussion. It has been designated as a National Important Folk Custom and draws large crowds each year.

**Yilan Toucheng Snatching the Lonely**: held annually at the end of lunar 7th in Toucheng, Yilan, this is Taiwan's most representative "Snatching the Lonely" ceremony. Banned during the Japanese colonial era and revived after WWII, it is now an internationally recognized folk event.

**Yunlin Douliu Da Zhong Temple "Mid-July Fire Walking"**: held on lunar 7/15, the temple hosts a fire-walking ceremony where devotees walk over coals — symbolizing the dispersal of impurity and welcoming peace.

The entire lunar 7th month, called "Ghost Month" in Taiwan, is the most active period for Da Zhong Ye worship. Temple ceremonies and household Pudu form a comprehensive folk system — a key field for studying traditional Taiwanese views on life, death, and community.

name: Door Gods
domain: Guarding doorways, warding off evil spirits
description: Walk into any Taiwanese temple and the first deities you "meet" aren't inside the hall — they're on the door panels: the Door Gods (Menshen). Taiwan's most common pair are two Tang Dynasty generals, Qin Shubao (white-faced, phoenix-eyed, wielding a mace) and Yuchi Gong (black-faced, fierce-eyed, wielding a steel whip), who by legend once stood guard against ghosts at Emperor Taizong's palace gate and were thereafter painted onto doors across the land. Beyond this "martial pair," Taiwanese tradition also knows civil-official Door Gods holding court tablets, the ancient pair Shentu and Yulei from the Classic of Mountains and Seas, "promotion and wealth" Door Gods, and the eunuch, palace-maid, and child Door Gods that guard rear and side halls. Painting a temple's Door Gods is one of Taiwan's most important traditional crafts — the works of masters such as Pan Lishui and Chen Yufeng are treated as a benchmark of a temple's artistic worth. For homes, Door Gods today are mostly printed posters, changed before Lunar New Year as part of the year-end ritual of sweeping out the old and welcoming the new. To read a temple, start with its doors — the quality of the Door Gods is often the temple's very face.
story:
The story of the Door Gods begins with an emperor who couldn't sleep.

Legend says that Emperor Taizong of Tang, Li Shimin, after years of war and much bloodshed, was tormented after taking the throne by the ghosts of the wronged crying for his life. He could not sleep, the court physicians' medicines did nothing, and affairs of state ground nearly to a halt.

The generals Qin Shubao and Yuchi Gong volunteered: in full armor, one to each side, they stood guard outside the imperial bedchamber all night long. Strangely enough, from that night the ghosts dared not come near, and Taizong at last slept soundly. But guarding night after night wore even these iron men down.

Unwilling to see his beloved generals exhausted, Taizong hit upon a plan: he ordered court painters to depict the two in their full martial array and had the portraits pasted on the bedchamber doors. From a distance the ghosts saw the images and still dared not approach. Word spread, and commoners rushed to copy it, pasting portraits of the two generals on their own doors — a custom that has held for more than a thousand years, right down to today's Lunar New Year.

An earlier tradition of Door Gods actually comes from the Classic of Mountains and Seas: beneath the great peach tree on Mount Dushuo in the Eastern Sea, the two gods Shentu and Yulei captured ghosts and fed them to a tiger. But for sheer drama, the Qin-Yuchi pairing — real generals "standing in" as paintings — sank deepest into people's hearts and became Taiwan's most popular Door Gods.
worship:
Household Door God posters follow a fixed schedule: after the "Sending Off the Gods" day on lunar 12/24 and before New Year's Eve, the old posters are torn down and burned and new ones pasted up, symbolizing the sweeping away of the old. There is one crucial taboo in pasting them — the two Door Gods must face each other (turned inward, looking toward one another) and must never be back-to-back, or folk belief holds they lose their protective power.

A temple's hand-painted Door Gods need no special daily worship, but every few years a master craftsman is invited to restore the painting; when a large temple is renovated, an "eye-opening" rite is performed in the old manner, dotting the eyes with vermilion ink to endow the Door Gods with spirit. Folk belief also holds that if a household suffers prolonged unrest, a Taoist priest may be invited to perform a rite before new Door Gods are pasted up, to expel foul influences and settle the home.

When you enter a temple, remember not to step on or linger on the threshold as you pass through the gate where the Door Gods stand watch; some temples keep the custom of men entering on the left and women on the right, matching the positions of the two martial Door Gods — the most basic courtesy you can show them.
festivals:
**Lunar New Year (Door God replacement period)**: Traditionally, Door God posters are replaced between the "Sending Off the Gods" day on the 24th of the 12th lunar month and New Year's Eve. This is one of the central rituals of the Taiwanese household year-end cleaning and decoration, alongside spring couplets, red envelopes, and the reunion dinner.

**Temple Door God Restoration Events**: In recent years, the Ministry of Culture and various municipal cultural departments have actively promoted restoration of traditional temple paintings. Some temples hold opening ceremonies after restoration, inviting the public to view newly restored Door God paintings. Notable examples include Bangka Longshan Temple, Dalongdong Baoan Temple, and Lukang Longshan Temple.

**Special Note**: Door Gods do not have a unified birthday celebration. As "functional" deities, their worship is incorporated into the broader rituals of their host temple or household — folk tradition rarely holds a celebration dedicated solely to Door Gods.
